WM Keyboard's look is driven by a theme: a full set of colors, gradients, key shapes and corner radii bundled together. Pick a built-in theme, let it follow your wallpaper, switch it automatically between day and night, or [build your own](/themes/editor/) from scratch.

<ThemePreview caption="A sample of built-in themes. Gradients, translucent keys, pill and cut key shapes, and a hue-cycling animation." />

## Choosing a theme

<SettingsPath path="Appearance / Keyboard themes" />

The theme gallery is a two-column grid: the **Default (system)** card first, then your saved custom themes (if you have any), then every built-in theme below them. Tapping a card applies it to the keyboard immediately.

The toolbox also has a **Themes** tool that draws live mini-previews right over the keys. It carries a shortlist rather than the whole gallery. Your custom and downloaded themes always show up in it, along with whichever built-ins you pin: each built-in card in the settings gallery carries a pin that adds it to the tool or takes it out, and a fresh install starts with a spread of six. That makes the tool a quick mood switch, with a handful of favourites to flip between mid-typing and the full collection one tap away in Settings (the tool's caption says so too). The tool runs full-bleed. The toolbar row hides while it's open and its space becomes a header, with a back button on the left and the **Themes** / **Icons** tabs beside it, so the cards get the reclaimed rows. It is read-only while Auto theme is on.

<PhoneFrame caption="The theme gallery: Default (system) first, then custom themes, then built-ins.">
  ![The theme gallery: custom themes on top, built-in themes below.](@assets/screens/themes/gallery-grid.webp)
</PhoneFrame>

There are 28 built-in themes. Eighteen are original WM Keyboard designs: plain colours like Ocean and Forest, gradient showcases like Nebula and the animated Sunset drift and Aurora, and two shape showcases (Bubble for pill keys, Facet for cut corners). The other ten (Dracula, Nord, Solarized Dark, Solarized Light, Catppuccin Mocha, Catppuccin Latte, Catppuccin Frappé, Catppuccin Macchiato, Tokyo Night, and Cyberpunk) are ports of well-known editor colour schemes, with Cyberpunk an original palette in that style. The MIT notices for the ones with upstream licences ship in the app's About screen.

They don't all get a card of their own, though. Twenty-two of the 28 belong to one of five families (Nightfall, Pastel, Gradients, Solarized and Catppuccin), and a family shows as a single card with one dot per look, so the grouped built-in grid is eleven cards rather than 28. [Theme families and looks](/themes/families/) covers the dots, the Grouped/Separate choice, and building a family of your own.

None of the built-in themes are editable in place. Opening one in the editor and changing anything duplicates it into a new custom theme first, so the originals stay put as a fallback you can always get back to. See [the theme editor](/themes/editor/) for building or duplicating a theme, [image backgrounds](/themes/backgrounds/) for putting a photo behind your keys, and [sharing themes](/themes/sharing/) for exporting, importing, and addon repositories.

## Matching your wallpaper

Turn on **Material You colors** and the **Default (system)** theme pulls its palette from your phone's wallpaper, the same way Android's own system UI does. It's on by default, and it only takes effect on Android 12 and up. The switch still shows on older versions, where it has nothing to do. Wallpaper color only ever applies to the Default theme, because every built-in and custom theme carries its own fixed palette regardless of this switch. The same toggle recolors the settings app as well as the keyboard.

## Dark mode and AMOLED

**Mode** is a four-way switch: System, Light, Dark, or Amoled. Like Material You colors, it controls both the settings app and the Default theme. Amoled always renders dark, and unlike System it doesn't wait on the phone's own light/dark setting. It forces the Default theme's board to pure black. Keys and other surfaces stay near-black blended tones rather than literal black, so key edges are still visible against that board. Built-in and custom themes ignore Mode entirely. If you want an AMOLED look on a fixed palette, the built-in **Pitch black** theme gets you there with its own true-black board.

<PhoneFrame caption="Mode set to Amoled: a true-black board under the Default theme.">
  ![Mode set to Amoled: a true-black board under the Default theme.](@assets/screens/themes/amoled-default-theme.webp)
</PhoneFrame>

## Switching automatically

**Auto (light + dark)** picks two themes (one for day, one for night) and swaps between them on its own, using one of three triggers:

- **System light/dark** follows the phone's own light/dark setting.
- **Time of day** switches at two clock times you set. It wraps across midnight correctly, so a schedule that starts light in the evening still works.
- **Sunrise & sunset** is computed on the device from the location saved in the weather tool, with no network round trip. Without a saved location, or on a polar day when the sun never rises or sets, this falls back to following the system setting.

While Auto is on, it owns the active theme completely: tapping a card in the gallery, or in the keyboard's own Themes tool, only previews it rather than switching to it. Turn Auto off to pick themes manually again.

<PhoneFrame caption="Auto theme on, with Sunrise & sunset chosen as the trigger.">
  ![Auto theme on, with Sunrise & sunset chosen as the trigger.](@assets/screens/themes/auto-theme-sun.webp)
</PhoneFrame>

## Options

<SettingsPath path="Appearance / Keyboard themes" />

- **Material You colors** (default on). Wallpaper-based dynamic color for the Default theme. It does nothing below Android 12, and nothing to built-in or custom themes.
- **Mode** (default System). Light, Dark, or Amoled, applied to the settings app and the Default theme.
- **Auto theme** (default off). Once on, pick a light theme, a dark theme, and a trigger (System light/dark, Time of day, or Sunrise & sunset). The time-of-day picker starts at 7:00 AM for the light theme and 7:00 PM for the dark theme.

Switching themes crossfades over about a third of a second, by hand or under Auto. Turning on **Reduce motion** (under accessibility) skips the crossfade and snaps instead.

## Details & edge cases

- **Contrast is worked out, not guessed.** A theme only has to specify a handful of required colors: board, key background, key text, accent. Anything left unset (popup colors, panel chip colors, tool-circle tints) is derived from what *is* set, using WCAG-style contrast math. That's why even a minimal two-color custom theme still has readable popups and legible active-tool highlights. The Default theme's dark mode goes further and steers clear of Material's own dark surface roles, which tend to flatten to near-identical grays. It blends the theme's text color over the darkened board at a few different strengths instead, which keeps panels and keys distinct.
- **That's separate from the accessibility contrast tools.** High contrast keys, key outlines, and color vision filters are a user-facing layer that overrides theme colors outright rather than filling in gaps. They live under Settings → Accessibility, not here. See [Accessibility](/accessibility/overview/) for those.
- **Key shape** is a per-theme setting with twelve options, picked from a list that draws each shape beside its name: Rounded (the default, and the one that follows the corner-radius value), Square, Pill, Cut (clamped to a 2–14dp radius regardless of the slider), Squircle, Arch, Leaf, Slanted, Hexagon, Scalloped, Ticket, and Circle (a typewriter-style round cap centred in the key). Everything except Rounded and Cut sizes itself off the key instead of the radius slider. Full table on [the theme editor page](/themes/editor/#key-shapes).
- **Corner radius has a global slider and an optional per-theme override.** The global **Key corner radius** slider (Appearance → Keys, default 8dp, range 0–28dp) applies unless a theme defines its own. The theme editor's "Theme-specific corner radii" toggle exposes separate sliders for key, popup, and tool-circle radius when you want a theme to ignore the global value.
- **Borders are opt-in and off by default.** A theme has no key border unless it sets one explicitly. The built-in Solarized Dark and Solarized Light themes show when a border earns its keep: their two background tones sit close enough in contrast that a thin outline keeps key edges readable. The toolbar tools have their own outline pair in the theme editor, off in the same way. The accessibility "Key outlines" toggle adds a border of its own to the keys and the tools, but only where the active theme hasn't already defined one. A theme's own border always wins.
- **No edition split.** Nothing on this page is gated: every built-in theme, gradient, animation, background image, and Material You itself works the same way in the full and lite editions.
